failure_modes: Generalising from three regimes and ten laboratory colonies to all collective behaviour
Total degree ignores direction, losing the difference between converging and diverging successions
Proximity-defined interactions inflate event counts in dense regimes such as aggression
Over-reading a good spectral collapse that is really a density effect
gloss: Collective regimes differ in how predictable the next interaction is, and only an order-keeping network shows it
invariants: Regimes are compared at matched interaction density, not by raw entropy
The same pipeline is applied to empirical and null trajectories
The signature is read from succession structure, so it disappears if order is aggregated away
mechanism: Build a {{second_order_network}} per short window (3 s), measure its {{degree_entropy}}, and place every window in an {{entropy_collapse}} against interaction density. Degree entropy here is the diversity of possible next interactions: high means many branching, merging successions (low predictability), low means few likely continuations. In fire ant colonies the regimes separated (GEE Wald chi^2(4) = 20.6, p = 0.0004) while the same measures on aggregated networks did not, as {{aggregation_blindness}} predicts. Roaming sat at low interaction density and low entropy density: sparse, predictable chains. As interaction density rises the regimes split: trailing at higher entropy density (branching, merging and redirection along trails) and aggression at lower (long-lived contact bouts with short inspection or avoidance events). A {{kinematic_null}} run through the same pipeline collapsed poorly (R^2 = 0.29 versus 0.68 empirical), so the signature reflects interaction rules and memory, not movement statistics. {{spectral_entropy}} on the same networks collapsed almost perfectly (R^2 = 0.999) but with near-zero exponents, i.e. it mostly tracked density.
preconditions: Identity-preserving tracking dense enough to resolve consecutive interactions
